title: Not knowing where I'm going
hookLine: his best-known prayer admits he doesn't know the road, but trusts the desire to please God pleases God

lines: HE DOESN'T KNOW WHERE HE'S GOING.
cards: So, what's the plan? The question shows up after graduation. After the divorce.
After the diagnosis, the layoff, the move. Sometimes there isn't one, and a confident answer at the family dinner covers the gap until the lights go out.

Thomas Merton, a well-known monk, a man people wrote to for spiritual advice, put on paper for anyone to read that he didn't know where he was going. That's the opening of a prayer he's remembered for.

teach.b: First, where it's from. The prayer sits in a small book called Thoughts in Solitude, published in 1958. It's short, a single paragraph.

teach.h: I DON'T SEE THE ROAD AHEAD.
teach.b: Merton tells God, in his own words, that he doesn't see the road ahead or know where it ends. He goes further: he doesn't really know himself, and thinking he's following God's will doesn't mean he actually is.
That's a startling thing for a monk to say. No false certainty at all. Third, the turn.
Then comes the line people hold onto.

teach.h: THE DESIRE TO PLEASE GOD PLEASES GOD.
teach.b: Merton says he believes that the desire to please God does in fact please God.

He hopes he has that desire in everything he does, and he trusts that if he keeps it, God will lead him by the right road, even when he can't tell. The desire counts, even when the map is missing. Fourth, the old roots.

Scripture has people who set out without a map. The Letter to the Hebrews says of Abraham, in the Douay-Rheims: "he went out, not knowing whither he went." And the psalm says: "Thy word is a lamp to my feet."

teach.h: A LAMP FOR THE NEXT STEP.
teach.b: It lights the next step, not the whole road. Merton isn't praising confusion.
He's saying faith can be honest: in his prayer, not knowing is allowed, as long as the wanting stays.

how: Some Catholics pray Merton's prayer from Thoughts in Solitude in times of discernment, and it appears on prayer cards and at retreats.

o: the ache of being lonely and left out
a monk's vow never to speak again
time alone by choice, often for prayer

games.q: the road ahead — tap the pairs.

s: Merton's prayer claims he knows God's plan for him
it admits he doesn't see the road, or even know himself.
the prayer trusts that wanting to please God already pleases God
that's the turn people hold onto.
a lamp in the psalm lights the whole road at once
a lamp lights the next step: "thy word is a lamp to my feet."

games.q: you don't know which way to go, and you're not even sure your own sense of God's will is right. what does Merton's prayer do?
o: wait to act until you're certain
trust that the desire to please God pleases God, and keep going
games.why: Merton admits he doesn't know, but trusts that the desire itself pleases God, and that God will lead him.

practice: Name one place in your life where you don't know the way, a decision, a relationship, a worry about what's next, and don't solve it; just admit it, quietly: I don't know.

Then notice whether, under the worry, there's a wanting: to do the right thing, to be good, to be close to God. If you pray, you can bring God both, the not-knowing and the wanting, in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Solitude, the book, Thoughts in Solitude, where Merton admitted he didn't know the road ahead, only the desire to please God. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the desire counts. The wanting can be enough for one day. Day two hundred eighty-one, done.
